source.title: VC Theoretical Explanation of Double Descent

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Reports results for randomly corrupted labels and their effect on double-descent curves, using random ReLU features with SVM and least-squares classifiers. This addresses label-noise degradation conceptually, but does not use the standard deep-network random-label experiment in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports Figure 3 results for randomly corrupted labels. Other cited random-label findings are prior work and are not recorded as results of this study. Figure 3 is supplied only as a caption and is not visually available, so no curve values or individual noise levels can be extracted.
record.test_reason: The label-corruption experiments use fixed random ReLU features with SVM or least-squares output classifiers, rather than standard deep networks trained by stochastic gradient methods. The SGD-trained deep-network experiments use clean labels. These results therefore do not test the specified versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate but incomplete: the authors argue that suitably applied VC bounds explain double descent, illustrate this with random-feature classifiers, and extend the approach to restricted SGD-trained multilayer settings using output-layer weight norms as a proposed proxy for VC dimension. They also report that label noise worsens second-descent generalization, which can become inferior to optimal first-descent performance.
record.recipe_differences: The label-noise experiments use a single-layer network with fixed random ReLU features and SVM or least-squares classifiers; they do not reproduce standard deep-network SGD fitting of fully random labels.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that the noise effect and interpolation threshold differ between SVM and least-squares classifiers.

fits_no_version.finding: For SVM and least-squares classifiers on fixed random ReLU features, increasing label noise increases weight norms and worsens second-descent test error. The interpolation threshold increases with noise for SVM but remains approximately 800 features for least squares.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fixed random-feature classifiers can interpolate corrupted labels, with noise-dependent generalization and classifier-dependent interpolation thresholds.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix A reports double-descent modeling for digit images with added Gaussian noise of standard deviation 0, 0.1, and 0.2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Double descent also occurs in random-feature classifiers trained on structured images corrupted by additive Gaussian noise.

record.peer_reviewed: Under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2023
record.problems: The label-noise outcomes are described qualitatively and shown only in Figure 3; the supplied text gives no exact noise levels or numerical curve values. The experiments use binary MNIST digit classification and random-feature classifiers, not standard deep networks trained on fully random labels.
record.rows_left_out: No rows extracted: the only relevant results are in Figure 3, whose caption and surrounding prose provide no recoverable values for separate noise conditions or a specific classifier-by-condition result. The text separately describes differing SVM and least-squares curve shapes, but does not provide values that can be assigned to rows.

untested.parts: Completely random labels fitted by standard deep networks with unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters, and chance-level test performance.
Training-time ratios and convergence slowdown as label corruption increases.

Deep-network fitting of shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or entirely Gaussian-noise inputs. Appendix A adds Gaussian noise to digit images; it does not replace images with unstructured inputs.

Perfect training fit and steadily worsening test error across a none-to-all label-corruption sweep in standard deep networks. The reported corruption sweep instead concerns fixed random-feature classifiers, and its full noise range and chance endpoint are unspecified.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and augmentation on random-label fitting, and generalization after removing these regularizers.
Temporal ordering of learning shared real-data patterns and memorizing label noise.

record.verdict_notes: No rows were supplied. The absence of numerical Figure 3 curves is not the decisive exclusion: the prose provides qualitative results, but the noisy-label experiments concern a different system class. The paper disputes interpretations of VC theory associated with the original source, rather than disputing the random-label fitting findings themselves.

versions.untested_parts: The reported labels are randomly corrupted, but the text does not state that a completely random labeling was tested or report the claimed standard deep-network setting.
Training time or convergence slowdown as a function of label corruption is not reported.
Shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, and Gaussian-noise inputs are not reported as training inputs fitted to zero error.

The paper reports test-error degradation with increasing label noise, but does not state that training error remains perfect across the noise sweep or that test error rises steadily toward chance. Figure 3's exact values and individual noise conditions are unavailable in the supplied text.
Weight decay, dropout, and data augmentation are not tested for their effects on random-label fitting or generalization.
The timing or order of learning real patterns and memorizing noise is not measured.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
